summary: Sirach 50 praises Simon son of Onias, the high priest, first for strengthening Jerusalem’s temple and defenses, then for the splendor of his public service at the altar. The chapter moves from Simon’s appearance and priestly ritual to the congregation’s worship, a blessing over Israel, a brief statement of hostility toward neighboring peoples, and the author’s closing claim about his book of wisdom.
whyItMatters: This chapter brings the long praise of Israel’s ancestors to its climax in the temple worship of Ben Sira’s own Jerusalem world. It also prepares for the book’s ending by naming the author and commending the instruction he has written.

context.author: Yeshua, or Jesus, son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his grandson later translated the Hebrew work into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jewish readers who received the grandson’s translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with the temple and priesthood central to public worship and Jewish scribal learning taking place in a Greek-speaking Mediterranean world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction that includes poetic praise, hymnic description, ancestral memory, prayer, and concluding exhortation.

outline.heading: Simon strengthens the temple and city
outline.note: Simon son of Onias is introduced as high priest and praised for repairing the house, strengthening the temple, preparing water storage, and fortifying the city against siege.

outline.heading: Simon appears in splendor
outline.note: The chapter compares Simon’s appearance to bright heavenly bodies, flowers, incense, gold, fruit trees, and a tall cypress.

outline.heading: The priestly service at the altar
outline.note: Simon puts on his robe, approaches the altar, receives portions from the priests, and pours out the libation at the foot of the altar.

outline.heading: The congregation worships
outline.note: The sons of Aaron sound trumpets, the people fall down in worship, singers praise, the people pray, and Simon blesses the congregation.

outline.heading: A blessing for Israel
outline.note: The speaker calls the hearers to bless God and asks for joy, peace, mercy, and deliverance in God’s time.

outline.heading: Enemies named and the book commended
outline.note: The chapter briefly names peoples that vex the speaker, then identifies Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar of Jerusalem as the writer and blesses the one who takes the instruction to heart.

keyVerses.text: It was Simon, the son of Onias, the high priest, who in his life repaired the house, and in his days strengthened the temple.
keyVerses.why: This opening identifies the central figure of the chapter and states why he is praised before the worship scene begins.

keyVerses.text: When he put on his glorious robe, and clothed himself in perfect splendor, ascending to the holy altar, he made the court of the sanctuary glorious.
keyVerses.why: This verse moves from comparisons describing Simon's splendor to his actions at the altar, showing how his priestly service brings glory to the sanctuary.

keyVerses.text: Then all the people together hurried, and fell down to the ground on their faces to worship their Lord, the Almighty, God Most High.
keyVerses.why: The focus widens from the high priest to the whole congregation, so the chapter’s praise of Simon is also a scene of public worship.

keyVerses.text: I have written in this book the instruction of understanding and knowledge, I Jesus, the son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem, who out of his heart poured forth wisdom.
keyVerses.why: Near the end of the chapter, the author names himself and describes the book as instruction shaped by wisdom.

themes: the high priest and the temple

questions.question: Who is Simon son of Onias in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter identifies Simon son of Onias as “the high priest” and praises him for repairing the temple, improving its water supply, and fortifying Jerusalem. Temple worship and the priesthood stood at the center of Ben Sira’s Jerusalem world. Simon is presented through his public works and his service at the altar.

questions.question: What is meant by “the house” and “the temple” here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “the house” is paired with “the temple” and “the temple enclosure,” so it refers to the temple complex in Jerusalem rather than an ordinary home. Simon is praised for strengthening and repairing it. The chapter treats this building work as part of his public importance.

questions.question: Why does the chapter use so many comparisons for Simon’s appearance?
questions.answer: Verses 5-10 pile up images of light, clouds, flowers, incense, gold, precious stones, and tall trees. The point is not to give a physical portrait in modern terms, but to present the high priest’s appearance during worship as glorious and beautiful. The comparisons belong to poetic praise.

questions.question: What is happening at the altar?
questions.answer: Simon is shown wearing his robe, ascending to the holy altar, receiving portions from the priests’ hands, and pouring out a cup of libation at the foot of the altar. The sons of Aaron hold the Lord’s offering, and the scene is described as the service at the altars. The chapter gives the reader a ceremonial sequence without explaining every ritual detail.

questions.question: Who are the “sons of Aaron”?
questions.answer: In this chapter, the “sons of Aaron” are the priests serving with Simon. They hold the Lord’s offering and later shout and sound trumpets. The phrase connects the temple service to priestly descent, but the chapter’s focus is on their role in the worship scene rather than on a genealogy.

questions.question: Does the chapter worship Simon?
questions.answer: No. Simon is praised in elevated language, but the people fall down “to worship their Lord, the Almighty, God Most High.” The singers praise God, the people pray to the Lord Most High, and Simon gives blessing in God’s name. The chapter honors the high priest as a leader in worship while directing worship to God.

questions.question: Why does the chapter suddenly speak against other peoples in verses 25-26?
questions.answer: After the blessing for Israel, the speaker says his soul is vexed with “two nations” and “the third,” then names those on the mountain of Samaria, the Philistines, and people in Shechem. The chapter does not explain the reasons for this hostility. Responsible readers should notice the sharp boundary language without turning the brief statement into a full history of these groups.

questions.question: Why does the author name himself here?
questions.answer: Verse 27 says, “I have written in this book,” and names “Jesus, the son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem.” This is unusual because many biblical books do not identify their author this directly. In Sirach, the named author fits the book’s character as instruction from a Jerusalem teacher.

questions.question: What does it mean to “exercise these things” and lay them up in the heart?
questions.answer: The final verses commend the reader who practices and stores up the instruction. “Exercise” here points to doing the teaching, not merely admiring it. The promised result in the chapter is becoming wise and being guided by “the light of the Lord.”

glossary.def: The leading priest in the temple service; in this chapter Simon son of Onias is praised in that role.
A poured offering; verse 15 describes Simon pouring out “the cup of the grape” at the foot of the altar.
A title for God used repeatedly in the worship scene and blessing.
The priests shown serving in the ritual, holding the offering and sounding trumpets.
A place named in the chapter’s brief statement of hostility toward neighboring peoples.
